title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system created a fabricated news article featuring a fake interview between Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock and ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never happened. The system generated false content that impersonated real public figures and was deployed in a scam to deceive potential investors.

This is a failure of AI used without human verification in the deployment phase. The system asserted false events as fact in a format designed to look like legitimate news. A human review before publication would have caught that the interview did not occur and that the quotes were invented. It is not established whether the people running the scam built this system themselves or used an existing AI tool.

The incident shows a pattern: AI systems are being used to rapidly generate convincing false content at scale for financial fraud. ASIC reports that such deepfake-based scams have risen sharply, with fake images, videos, and fabricated articles impersonating politicians and financial experts. Detecting and stopping these requires either verification that sources exist before content is published, or rapid takedown once false content is identified.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
A fake online article featured Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock in a fabricated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler, where she allegedly confronted him about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred, but was created as part of an increasingly sophisticated scam using artificial intelligence. ASIC reports that such deepfake-based investment schemes are rising rapidly, with these scams using fake images, videos, and fabricated news articles featuring celebrities and politicians to deceive potential investors.

Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams, representing a 182 percent increase. The regulator took down 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese tops the list of impersonated figures, followed by politicians and financial experts including Alan Kohler, who has been targeted multiple times. ASIC advises consumers to verify Australian Financial Services licence numbers through official registers and avoid websites that cannot provide legitimate credentials. The regulator is increasing enforcement efforts, though finance presenter Kohler argues platforms and AI companies should face heavy fines for facilitating these scams.
